store.0: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year. My schedule this semester is quite packed, but it's exciting to be taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to think about how far I've come since my freshman year, when I was learning about basic data structures. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even exploring the basics of quantum computing. It's amazing to see how quickly time has passed.

store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm a huge fan of theory when it connects directly to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. The problems we explore in this class are fascinating, and we've been diving into dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It can be mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is great at explaining these complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll often write a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to at least approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing with ideas.

store.4: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, I'm also taking a Distributed Systems course(CS 2631), which is probably the second most challenging. It involves a lot of reading, group discussions, and a major project where we're simulating a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. However, that's also the beauty of it. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures gracefully. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a single misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.

store.6: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. To be honest, I've always been a gamer at heart, so this was a must-take. The professor is actually from the industry; he worked on a couple of indie games that got some decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, how to implement physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's unbelievably fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was tricky, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.

store.8: I'm also taking an Introduction to Quantum Computing class, which sounds cutting-edge, I know. Initially, it was intimidating, but the professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff and has made me rethink how I approach problems.

store.10: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a nice change of pace from all the coding in my other classes. It's great to just sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and it was fascinating to research. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.

store.12: My schedule is pretty packed, as you can imagine. Mondays and Wednesdays are the busiest days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter, with Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be tough if I'm already tired from the day. Fridays are a bit more relaxed, with no scheduled classes, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or lab work. I also do some undergraduate research hours in a lab that's focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to stay on top of everything and make the most of my senior year.

store.14: The biggest challenge this semester is definitely balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and that's without considering any major bugs or issues with the model. The Distributed Systems project is another significant time sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. However, coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a mini-nightmare. Despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of a real job environment. I'm grateful for the opportunity to dive deep and explore these complex topics.

store.16: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, especially if something's due the next day and I'm stuck debugging. However, it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know that if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway for me is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
